newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MANDELA SIGNS S.AFRICA CONSTITUTION AT SHARPEVILLE.
newsitem.headline: MANDELA SIGNS S.AFRICA CONSTITUTION AT SHARPEVILLE.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela will sign on Tuesday South Africa's post-apartheid constitution guaranteeing racial and social equality, the final product of years of political wrangling in smoke-filled rooms.
The document was agreed on by the main players in more than half a decade of talks between Mandela's ANC and the National Party of the country's last white president, F.W. de Klerk.
The ceremony takes place in Sharpeville where 69 black demonstrators were killed by police in 1960.
Shortly after the massacre, white-ruled South Africa shook a defiant fist at a horrified world and retreated into the laager for another 30 years of minority rule.
The African National Congress was banned and set up office in exile and took up arms. A few years later Mandela and most of his senior colleagues were arrested and jailed.
Armed supporters flowed into the country to take on the apartheid state and later international sanctions increased the pressure on the white government to talk to its enemies.
That process began in 1990 when de Klerk released Mandela from jail and unbanned the ANC, which became the country's ruling party in elections four years later.
Negotiations began in complicated South African fashion with "talks about talks'' followed by deadlines set in stone which were then ignored.
Every twist and turn of the tortuous process was bannered in local newspapers as a "breakthrough'' or "disaster''.

The mainly Zulu Inkatha Freedom Party, wanting strong regional powers, initially took part in the talks but left the final negotiations when it said it became clear that promises made by other parties would not be honoured.
Politicians hailed the constitution as a victory over many other setbacks too when it was finished this year.

Those included a brief ANC withdrawal over continued violence in the country, the invasion of the talks by armed right-wingers trying to stave off majority rule and temporary rejection by the Constitutional Court, the highest in the land.
Last week the court gave the rejigged document the seal of approval and Mandela said it would be fitting to sign it into law on international human rights day.
